turning_points.label: Demobilisation
turning_points.title: Post-war demobilisation
turning_points.description: Defence outlays fell from 37% of GDP to under 5% in three years. Combined with 1946-48 inflation, which cut the real value of the debt stock by roughly a third, the ratio fell faster than any deliberate repayment could have achieved.

turning_points.label: Medicare/Medicaid
turning_points.title: Social Security Act Amendments of 1965
turning_points.description: Created Medicare and Medicaid as open-ended fee-for-service entitlements with no dedicated actuarial pre-funding. The cost showed up decades later, which is exactly why a contemporaneous index registers almost nothing here.

turning_points.label: Bretton Woods ends
turning_points.title: Suspension of gold convertibility
turning_points.description: Ended the dollar's gold peg and removed the external constraint on monetary expansion. The 1972 Social Security amendments added automatic CPI indexing on a formula that over-corrected for inflation until it was repaired in 1977.

turning_points.label: ERTA
turning_points.title: Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981
turning_points.description: Cut marginal rates 23% across the board while defence spending rose to 6.1% of GDP. Establishes the modern pattern of large structural deficits at full employment, visible here as the first sustained peacetime rise in the interest burden.

turning_points.label: PAYGO
turning_points.title: Budget Enforcement Act of 1990
turning_points.description: Introduced statutory PAYGO and discretionary caps. With the 1993 OBRA rate increases and the late-1990s productivity acceleration, this produced the only sustained surpluses in the post-war record.

turning_points.label: PAYGO lapses
turning_points.title: EGTRRA and the expiry of statutory PAYGO
turning_points.description: PAYGO was allowed to expire, the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts passed without offsets, and Medicare Part D was added in 2003 with no dedicated financing. The projected surplus reverted to structural deficit within two years.

turning_points.label: GFC
turning_points.title: Financial crisis and the zero-rate era
turning_points.description: The debt ratio roughly doubled, but near-zero policy rates held the effective cost of the stock down: r − g stayed firmly negative for a decade, which is why the interest burden fell while the debt rose.

turning_points.label: Rate shock
turning_points.title: Post-COVID inflation and the end of free debt
turning_points.description: 525bp of tightening from 2022 repriced the stock as it rolled over. Net interest went from $352bn in FY2021 to over $1tn in FY2025, passing total defence outlays — the single largest change in the fiscal block in the series.

projections.label: Favourable
projections.narrative: Rates stay near today's effective cost while nominal growth runs at the pre-2008 trend, and the primary deficit is halved to 1.5% of GDP. r − g stays negative, so the debt ratio erodes on its own.

projections.label: Baseline
projections.narrative: The effective rate on the stock converges upward to 4.3% as low-coupon debt from the 2010s rolls off, nominal growth settles at 4.0%, and the primary deficit holds near its current 3% of GDP. r − g turns mildly positive.

projections.label: Adverse
projections.narrative: Term premia rebuild, the effective rate reaches 5.5%, nominal growth slows to 3.5% on demographic drag, and the primary deficit widens to 4.5% as retirement and health outlays land. r − g sits at +2pp and the ratio compounds.

thresholds.label: Crowding-out
thresholds.desc: Debt service exceeds all non-defence discretionary spending.

thresholds.label: Distress zone
thresholds.desc: The band where rating agencies have historically downgraded sovereigns.

thresholds.label: Fiscal dominance
thresholds.desc: Debt service crowds out the discretionary budget entirely; monetary policy loses independence.

quadrant_counts.name: Compounding
quadrant_counts.desc: r > g and a primary deficit. Both terms push the ratio up; it rises with no new policy at all.

quadrant_counts.name: Outgrowing the deficit
quadrant_counts.desc: A primary deficit absorbed by favourable dynamics. Durable only while r stays below g.

quadrant_counts.name: Consolidating
quadrant_counts.desc: Primary surplus and r < g. Both terms cut the ratio — the post-war and late-1990s configuration.

quadrant_counts.name: Running to stand still
quadrant_counts.desc: A primary surplus spent offsetting adverse dynamics. Real austerity, little improvement in the ratio.

schemes.label: Balanced (published index)
schemes.desc: 50% fiscal / 30% growth / 20% monetary — the weighting used everywhere else on this page.

schemes.label: Fiscal-heavy
schemes.desc: 65% fiscal / 20% growth / 15% monetary — a pure solvency reading.

schemes.label: Growth-heavy
schemes.desc: 35% fiscal / 45% growth / 20% monetary — treats productive capacity as the binding constraint.

schemes.label: Equal weights
schemes.desc: One seventh each — the naive benchmark, included because it embeds no judgement at all.

quadrant.name: Outgrowing the deficit
quadrant.desc: A primary deficit absorbed by favourable dynamics. Durable only while r stays below g.

fiscal_dominance.label: Fiscal dominance
fiscal_dominance.desc: Debt service crowds out the discretionary budget entirely; monetary policy loses independence.

entries.name: One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1)
entries.source: CBO final score; extension estimate from CRFB
entries.note: The single largest fiscal action in the series' recent history. CBO's $3.4tn is the primary-deficit effect; $4.1tn includes the debt service it generates. Neither figure includes macroeconomic feedback, which CRFB expects would add to borrowing rather than offset it.

entries.name: Iran conflict (Operation Epic Fury)
entries.source: OMB testimony (30 June 2026) and CSIS analysis (July 2026)
entries.note: OMB puts direct war costs near $30bn; CSIS estimates ~$40bn including base repair. The $87.6bn supplemental request is broader than the war — roughly a third is war-related, the rest is other defence priorities and unrelated agency funding.

entries.name: FY2026 national defence budget
entries.note: National defence passed $1tn for the first time in FY2026, up more than 13% on FY2025, with $1.5tn requested for FY2027. In share-of-GDP terms — the measure that matters for solvency — this is still near the lowest of the whole post-war record.
